column1: Use AI to generate architecture diagrams

Many applications are missing key architecture diagrams including:

* System architecture - high level view of all software, hardware, dependencies
* Application architecture - Internal structure of the application
* Network diagram - Routers, LBs and firewalls

reference docs (in ESDC SharePoint):

* [https://014gc.sharepoint.com/:p:/r/sites/BAI-CBO/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7BF7535318-885E-4F0B-8BF4-EAA1E6FE9B50%7D&file=2026-01-09%20-%20Chainguard-Trusted-Base-Container-Images.pptx&action=edit&mobileredirect=true&DefaultItemOpen=1|https://014gc.sharepoint.com/:p:/r/sites/BAI-CBO/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7BF7535318-885E-4F0B-8BF4-EAA1E6FE9B50%7D&file=2026-01-09%20-%20Chainguard-Trusted-Base-Container-Images.pptx&action=edit&mobileredirect=true&DefaultItemOpen=1|smart-link] 
* Signed- Directive on Container Image Security - Final

h3. Chainguard in IITB:

* ESDC already recommends using Chainguard hardened base images for our department, it’s already been approved with Governance
* SSC already has a limited set of chainguard base images (SSC Aurora team) available to all departments by using a pull token & internal pull-through registry (using either Nexus Repository Manager or JFrog)
* SSC already has a cost-recovery model to fund Chainguard images (to avoid duplication of costs and registry setup)
* the pull-through method has already been tested successfully using Nexus Repository Manager to create a mirror image registry and it’s available for use
* Nexus is the IT Security approved tool (JFrog has NOT been approved)
* containers should NOT be restricted through cloud (they should also be available to use on desktops)

h3. Chainguard vs other hardened images:

!2026jul10-compare-hardened-containers-20260710-141025.png|width=942,alt="2026jul10-compare-hardened-containers-20260710-141025.png"!

h3. Current Problems:

* none of the IITB directorates can agree on who should/can take ownership of this process:
** identify a short list of ESDC-preferred Chainguard base images
** negotiate shared funding with SSC to use this
** make these Chainguard images available internally through an ESDC-supported container registry
** provide guidance on how to use and recommended expectations to dev teams
* this process seems to affect many groups (Operations, IT Security, ECS, OCMC, SADE?) 
* the longer it takes for the directorates to agree on a decision, the more it will push individual dev teams find their own way of containerizing their apps (ie, using unhardened base images that could cause security vulnerabilities)

h3. Next Steps:

* to discuss with ARO team:
** do we want to take ownership of this for ESDC? *No*
** is this in our Containerization scope? Should we be responsible for maintaining this? *No, the decision is up to IT Security, ECS, SADE?*
** or do we want to just help push this forward so dev teams can start using it? *We may push this up to our executive to push this initiative forward.*

column1: Find out what is blocking containerization in IITB
column26:
Even if ARO can create secure (hardened) base images for dev teams to use, they can’t install Docker or other software they need to build their own containers.

Find out what the root problem is to allow dev teams to build & deploy their own containerized apps:

* developers who have admin(developer) rights on their laptops are no longer allowed to install the software they need (ie, Docker, Podman, Copilot, Chainguard, etc…) since the IITB Secure Teleworking Policy
* Macbooks are not yet available for developers to use as their off-network laptops
* developers are given refurbished off-network laptops to install & setup themselves (ie, 10+ different Linux distributions to install, install MS Defender, etc…)
* do dev teams still need to manage their security certificates? Could this be solved by using containers? Or is this an unrelated problem (install MS Defender on all workstations)?  
* do dev teams still need to scan their apps for vulnerabilities in their software supply chain? Could this be solved by using containers?

08/Sep/26 7:03 PM;70121:413fb3f3-84b2-40e4-9f69-28d1ea482c93;{{> ill level with you here, I know literally nothing about this app. do the suggestions made within seem likely to help? sounds like the app is fine day-to-day, but during crunch season (January-June) when their clients submit large csv files and theyre uploaded into the system, it crashes. answer like im an executive}}

Straight answer: yes, the suggestions are aimed at the right target, and the symptom you describe actually makes the case stronger than the report alone does.

h2. Why this rings true

Your description — fine day-to-day, falls over in Jan–June when clients push big files in at the same time — is a classic *memory-and-concurrency* failure, not a "the app is badly written everywhere" problem. Day-to-day, one user does one thing at a time and the system copes. In crunch season you get *large files × many at once*, and several of the confirmed findings stack up exactly under those conditions:

* Each upload loads the *entire file into memory* at once. Ten uploads = ten full files in memory.
* The app writes records *one at a time*, so each upload holds a database connection for a long time. Many at once drains the connection pool.
* A shared database routine *runs every read twice* and pulls full result sets into memory — invisible day-to-day, meaningful under load.
* The safeguard meant to stop two imports overlapping *doesn't reliably work*.

None of those bite when it's quiet. All of them bite hardest exactly when you say it breaks. That alignment is why I'd treat these as credible causes, not guesses.

h2. My honest read on the fixes

* *Likely to help, and mostly low-risk:* capping concurrent imports, streaming files instead of loading them whole, and batching the writes go straight at memory and connection pressure — the two things most likely killing you in crunch. Fixing the "runs twice" defect is cheap and helps everywhere.
* *The one caveat:* code review can tell you _where the pressure is_, but it can't prove _which straw breaks the camel's back_. The good news is that proving it is fast and cheap — reproduce a few concurrent large uploads in a test environment and watch memory and connections. That one test, done before touching code, tells you whether you're fixing the real thing.

h2. What I'd tell the board

# This looks like a *capacity/concurrency* problem with identifiable, fixable causes — not a rewrite.
# Spend a *small amount* to measure it first (days, not months). Cheap insurance against fixing the wrong thing.
# Then do the *contained fixes* (limit overlap, stream files, batch writes). Most can be done inside WEIMS without touching shared code — lower risk than it sounds.
# Keep the *"two new equity groups"* work on a *separate track*. It's a genuine redesign and shouldn't ride on the stability fixes or vice versa.

Bottom line: the recommendations are sensible and proportionate, and they're pointed at the conditions you actually see failing. I wouldn't authorize a big rebuild. I'd fund a short measurement step, then the targeted fixes — that's the high-confidence, low-regret path.





h1. PUT EVEN SIMPLER:

h2. The problem in one line

The system is fine most of the year. It crashes in Jan–June because too many big files get uploaded at the same time and it runs out of room to handle them.

h2. Think of it like a checkout line

* Normal months = one shopper, one cashier. No problem.
* Crunch season = a hundred shoppers show up at once, and the cashier scans *one item at a time* while holding everyone else up.
* Eventually the store gets so crowded nobody can move. That's the crash.

h2. Do the fixes make sense?

Yes. The team found the real bottlenecks, and the fixes go straight at them:

* *Let fewer files process at once* so the "store" doesn't overcrowd.
* *Scan items in bulk instead of one at a time* so each upload finishes faster.
* *Stop wasting space* (there's a bug making the system do some work twice).

These are targeted repairs, not a rebuild.

h2. What I'd tell an executive

* It's a *traffic jam problem*, not a broken-app problem.
* Spend a little time to *confirm it in a test* first (cheap, quick).
* Then do the *small fixes*. Low risk, likely big relief in crunch season.
* The *"two new groups"* request is a separate job — don't bundle it with this.

Bottom line: *worth doing, low risk, no big rebuild needed.*

column1: Establish an Enterprise GitHub Copilot Community of Practice
column26:
*Title:* Establish an Enterprise GitHub Copilot Community of Practice

*As an* ARO team member responsible for AI enablement and governance,

*I want* to establish and facilitate a GitHub Copilot Community of Practice (CoP) for all ESDC teams holding GitHub Copilot licenses,

*So that* teams can share their use cases, lessons learned, successes, and challenges, enabling the ARO and SRE teams to identify, assess, and promote effective and secure GitHub Copilot practices across ESDC.

----

h3. Business Value

The Community of Practice will create a structured forum for knowledge sharing and continuous improvement, ensuring that investments in GitHub Copilot generate maximum value. Insights gathered from participating teams will help establish enterprise-approved use cases, identify risks and common errors, improve developer productivity, and support the development of guidance, standards, and best practices for GitHub Copilot adoption within ESDC.

----

h3. Acceptance Criteria

# A GitHub Copilot Community of Practice is established and administered by the ARO team.
# Participation is mandatory for all ESDC teams with one or more GitHub Copilot licenses.
# CoP sessions are held on a recurring basis (e.g., monthly or quarterly).
# Participating teams present:
#* Current GitHub Copilot use cases.
#* Measurable benefits and outcomes achieved.
#* Challenges encountered.
#* Mistakes, failures, or lessons learned.
# The ARO and SRE teams review information presented during CoP sessions to:
#* Identify successful enterprise use cases.
#* Assess risks and operational impacts.
#* Determine patterns of misuse or ineffective implementation.
#* Develop recommendations and best practices.
# A repository of presentations, lessons learned, and approved use cases is maintained and made accessible to participants.
# Enterprise guidance and recommended GitHub Copilot use cases are updated based on CoP findings and shared with all participating teams.
# Attendance and participation metrics are tracked and reported.

----

h3. Definition of Done

* Community of Practice governance and operating model are defined.
* Initial participant roster of licensed teams is established.
* First CoP session is conducted.
* Documentation repository is available.
* Process for capturing and evaluating lessons learned is implemented.
* Initial set of recommended GitHub Copilot use cases and best practices is published by the ARO and SRE teams.

*As an* ARO service owner,

*I want* to perform an initial investigation into the feasibility, benefits, risks, and implementation considerations of a self-hosted Large Language Model (LLM),

*So that* I can determine whether a self-hosted AI capability can support AIM use cases while meeting organizational requirements for security, privacy, governance, and operational sustainability.

*Vision*

Establish a foundational understanding of how self-hosted LLM technologies could support AIM service objectives, including knowledge discovery, application analysis, document summarization, service intelligence, and automation.

The investigation will provide sufficient information to make an informed decision on whether to proceed with a proof-of-concept, leverage an existing enterprise AI platform, or defer investment.

*Acceptance Criteria*

||ID||Acceptance Criteria||Expected Outcome||
|AC1|A list of candidate self-hosted LLM solutions is documented.|Potential technology options are identified.|
|AC2|Key AIM use cases suitable for LLM enablement are identified and documented.|Investigation is aligned to business needs.|
|AC3|Security, privacy, data residency, and governance considerations are documented.|Risks and constraints are understood.|
|AC4|Infrastructure and hosting requirements are assessed at a high level.|Technical feasibility is understood.|
|AC5|Integration considerations with existing AIM services and repositories are documented.|Dependencies and complexity are identified.|
|AC6|Benefits, risks, assumptions, and limitations for each option are evaluated.|Stakeholders can make informed decisions.|
|AC7|A comparison matrix of candidate solutions is produced.|Options can be evaluated consistently.|
|AC8|A recommendation is provided regarding next steps (POC, Pilot, Further Investigation, or No-Go).|Clear direction is established.|
|AC09|Investigation outcomes are documented in a decision brief or presentation.|Results are available for future planning activities.|

1-2 minutes – Context

* Not identifying staffing requirements for next year. Trying to understand what capabilities will be required in AIM next 3 years, what risks we are facing

15 minutes – Current state (looking for points of failure, burnout, legacy systems)

* What work is becoming more difficult to deliver?
* Where are you seeing increasing demand?
* Where are you relying on a small number of experts?   Do you have the experts?
* What worries you most if a key employee leaves tomorrow?

15 minutes – Future State

* What will your team look like in 3 years?  (does this mean resource numbers?   Also, given the stabilization exercise, this will change for some;  they may not know what there team will look like in six months)
* What technologies will have the greatest impact ?  ( I think we need to expand this;  greatest impact on AIM/ ESDC / on how we prioritize./ deliver?  We can just give a bit more context – and the open ended questions are good)
* What capabilities do you think AIM is underinvesting in today?
* What skills do we need to start building now?

5 minutes – Solutions

* If it were up to you, what would you do first?  (for our notes we could ask also,  what would your advice be of where we spend our first dollar? It makes people really think about prioritizing and where we would get value for money).
* What could we solve through development rather than recruitment?   Great question!
* Where could teams share expertise more effectively?  How?

5 minutes – Prioritization

* If you could choose only three workforce investments for AIM over the next three years, what would they be?  (this may be difficult to answer as some of it comes our way;  but ok with the question);

5 minutes – Heat Map

* Ask every participant to rate each capability using a simple heat map (these topics should be updated based on the questionnaire in step 1):

|*Capability*|*Importance in 3 Years*|*AIM Capability Today*|
|AI|High|Low|
|Automation|High|Medium|
|Cloud|High|Medium|
|Cybersecurity|High|Medium|
|SRE|High|High|
|Legacy Systems|Medium|High|

* Create a master capability framework
** Technical capabilities
*** AI
*** Automation
*** Cloud engineering
*** Software Development
*** Etc.
** Workforce capabilities
*** Leadership
*** Project Delivery
*** Vendor Management
*** Business Analysis
*** Etc.
* Capture interview data consistently
** Team Name
** Current Gaps
** Future capabilities Required
** Workforce Risks
** Suggested Actions
** Notable Quotes

** Tab 1: Capability Gaps

* Create a Heat Map
** Take heatmap results and change into numerical value :
*** Importance in 3 years, 1= low, 2=medium, 3=high
*** Current AIM Capability, 1= low, 2=medium, 3=high

|*Capability*|*Future Importance*|*Current Strength*|
|AI|3|1|
|Automation|3|2|
|Cloud|3|2|
|Cybersecurity|3|2|
|Legacy Systems|2|3|

*** Then average scores across all teams:

|*Capability*|*Future Importance*|*Current Strength*|*Gap*|
|AI|2.9|1.2|1.7|
|Automation|2.8|1.7|1.1|
|Cloud|2.8|1.9|0.9|

*** Largest gap becomes workforce priorities – +turns something subjective into something measurable+

The workshop should ideally produce inputs that can go directly into HR Plan

Objectives:

* Critical capabilities AIM needs over the next 3 years
* Most significant workforce risks
* Largest skill gaps
* Highest-priority actions
* Ownership for next steps

Duration: 2-3 hours

Agenda:

* Part 1: Present findings (30 mins)
** Top Capability Gaps
** Top Workforce Risks
** Top Solutions suggested
* Part 2: Validate Priorities (45 mins)
** Present capabilities heat maps
** Questions:
*** Which capability gaps pose greatest risk to our success?
*** Which capabilities are mission-critical?
*** Which capabilities can we buy versus build? (e.g. Hire or retrain?)
*** Which capability gaps require immediate attention?
** Ask participants to identify top 5 capability priorities
*** Do we use a tool like a word map for this? Have an open questionnaire during a meeting to view results?
* Part 3: Workforce risks (30 mins)
** What workforce risks keep you awake at night?
** What expertise would be most difficult to replace?
** What knowledge is vulnerable to departure or retirement?
** Where are we overly dependent on individuals?
** Which risks are increasing?
** Can build a matrix to represent this data, objective is identifying the risks that matter most

|** *Risk*|** *Likelihood*|** *Impact*|
|** Retirement|** High|** High|
|** Recruitment|** High|** High|
|** Burnout|** Medium|** High|
|** Succession|** High|** High|

* Part 4 – Solutions workshop **THE MOST IMPORTANT PART** (45 mins)
** _Shift conversation from headcount to capability strategy_
** Build
*** Which capabilities should AIM develop internally?
** Buy
*** Which capabilities should AIM recruit for?
** Borrow
*** Which capabilities could be obtained through partnerships or temporary resources?
** Automation
*** Which workforce pressures can be reduced through automation or AI?
* Part 5 – Prioritization (30 mins)
** Ask: If AIM could only fund three workforce initiatives, what should they be?
*** Examples:
**** Technical leadership program
**** AI upskilling strategy
**** Knowledge transfer initiative
**** Succession planning framework
**** Cloud recruitment strategy
** Ask: What capabilities must AIM have in three years that, if we fail to develop them, would significantly affect our ability to deliver our mandate?

 

Deliverables: Executive summary describing AIM workforce priorities for the next 3 years.  (this will be a key piece of the HR plan)

* Example:

* *Priority Capability Areas*
** AI and Automation
** Platform Engineering and Cloud
** Cybersecurity
** Technical Leadership
** Knowledge Transfer
* *Priority Workforce Risks*
** Knowledge concentration
** Recruitment challenges
** Retirement exposure
** Succession planning gaps
* *Priority Actions*
** Directorate-wide AI upskilling strategy
** Structured knowledge-transfer program
** Technical talent pipeline and recruitment plan
** Technical leadership development program
** Communities of practice and cross-training

column1: Create Client Intake Questionnaire for AIS Code Analysis Requests
column26:
*As an* ARO team member,
*I want* clients requesting an AIS code analysis to complete a standardized intake questionnaire that is accessible from the ARO SharePoint site,
*So that* the ARO team can consistently collect all required information before beginning an analysis and automatically store the responses in a SharePoint list for tracking and reporting purposes.

----

h3. Description

Develop a questionnaire that captures the standard intake information required by the ARO team before conducting an AIS code analysis. The questionnaire will be available to clients through an approved form solution (e.g., Microsoft Forms) and must be accessible through a prominent link on the ARO SharePoint site.

Upon submission, all responses must be automatically transferred to a SharePoint list. The SharePoint list will serve as the authoritative repository for intake data and will support request management, reporting, and future analytics.

----

h3. Acceptance Criteria

h4. AC1: Questionnaire Creation

* A questionnaire is created containing all standard AIS code analysis intake questions defined by the ARO team.
* All mandatory questions are clearly identified and require a response before submission.
* Questionnaire language is clear and understandable for clients.

h4. AC2: SharePoint Site Access

* A link to the questionnaire is available on the ARO SharePoint site.
* The link is easily discoverable by clients requesting AIS code analysis services.
* Selecting the link opens the questionnaire without requiring additional navigation steps.

h4. AC3: Submission Validation

* Clients can successfully submit the questionnaire once all mandatory fields are completed.
* Users receive a confirmation message upon successful submission.

h4. AC4: SharePoint Integration

* Each questionnaire submission automatically creates a new item in the designated SharePoint list.
* All questionnaire responses are mapped to the appropriate SharePoint list columns.
* The integration occurs without manual intervention.

h4. AC5: Data Integrity

* Submitted responses are accurately transferred to the SharePoint list.
* No data is lost, truncated, or incorrectly mapped during transfer.

h4. AC6: Security and Access

* Access to submitted responses in the SharePoint list is restricted to authorized ARO personnel.
* Client-submitted data is stored in accordance with departmental information management and security requirements.

h4. AC7: Reporting and Tracking

* The SharePoint list captures the submission date and time.
* Each submission is assigned a unique identifier for tracking purposes.
* ARO team members can view and sort submissions within the SharePoint list.

----

h3. Definition of Done

* Questionnaire has been reviewed and approved by the ARO team.
* Questionnaire link has been added to the ARO SharePoint site.
* SharePoint list has been created and configured.
* Automated transfer of questionnaire responses to SharePoint has been tested successfully.
* End-to-end testing confirms all intake responses are captured accurately.
* Documentation is provided for maintenance and future updates to the questionnaire.

* AIS Backlog (public)

h2. Form settings

* Name: Application Intelligence Service Intake
* Who can respond: Only people in the organization
* Record name: On
* One response per person: Off, one client may submit several applications
* Group ownership: Put the Form under the ARO M365 group rather than one person’s personal Forms area

----

h2. Form

Use this Form to request an Application Intelligence Service assessment.

The information will help us identify the application, access the appropriate source repositories, understand the questions you need answered, and prepare the assessment.

Provide only information appropriate for internal departmental use. Do not include passwords, access tokens, production credentials, classified information, protected data extracts, source-code excerpts, or personal information about application users.

After submission, the AIS team will review the request and contact you.

----

h2. Section 1: Application

# Application name
What is the application’s official name?
(Required, short text)
# Acronym
What acronym or short name is commonly used?
(Optional, short text)
# Business area
Which business area is responsible for the application?
(Required, short text)
# Contacts
Who should we contact about this assessment?
(Required, long text;
Help text: Provide the names and organizational email addresses for the business contact, technical contact, and any other relevant contact)

----

h2. Section 2: Assessment need

# Business purpose
What does the application do?
(Required, long text;
Help text: In a few sentences, describe the business process or service supported by the application.)
# Reason for the request
Why are you requesting an AIS assessment?
(Required, multiple choice)

* Understand or document the application
* Investigate performance or stability
* Investigate security or supportability
* Prepare for modernization or migration
* Understand technical debt
* Capture critical knowledge
* Assess a proposed business or technical change
* Support planning or investment discussions
* Other

# Key questions
What are the most important questions you need the assessment to answer?
(Required, long text;
Help text: Focus on the problems, changes, or decisions the assessment should support)
# Known concerns
Are there known problems, risks, upcoming changes, or important limitations?
(Optional, long text;
Help text: Include observed performance problems, outages, difficult support areas, aging technologies, undocumented dependencies, knowledge gaps, or planned changes. Distinguish observed behaviour from suspected causes where possible)
# Priority workflows
Which application workflows should the assessment prioritize?
(Optional, long text;
Help text: Examples include submitting an application, processing an annual file, calculating eligibility, approving a request, generating a report, or exchanging information with another system)

----

h2. Section 3: Source readiness

# Primary repository
Provide the URL for the primary application repository.
(Required, short text;
Help text: Paste the full GitHub or Azure DevOps repository URL. Do not include a password or access token)
# Branch, tag, or release
Which branch, tag, or release should be assessed?
(Required, short text)
# Other repositories
Are there other repositories that should be included?
(Required, Choice: Yes, No;
Help text: Include database schemas, stored procedures, APIs, deployment projects, shared libraries, scheduled jobs, reporting projects, test repositories, etc.)
If Yes:
List each repository, its purpose, and the branch or release to assess.
# Database source
Are the application database schema and stored procedures available?
(Required, multiple choice)

* Yes, included above
* Yes, but access must be arranged
* No
* The application does not use a database
* Not sure

----

h2. Section 4: Boundaries and timing

# Documentation
Provide links to any useful documentation.
(Optional, long text;
Help text: Include links to architecture diagrams, runbooks, business rules, interface specifications, security assessments, privacy assessments, accessibility reviews, and previous modernization work where available)
# Restrictions
Are there any access restrictions, sensitive areas, or files that AIS must exclude?
(Required, long text;
Help text: Enter None known if there are no known restrictions. Do not include passwords, credentials, or sensitive data in the response)
# Timing
Is this assessment connected to a target date or upcoming decision?
(Required, Yes or No)
If Yes:

* What is the requested date?
* What decision or activity does the assessment support?

# Public backlog summary
Provide a short, non-sensitive description we may display in the internal AIS backlog.
(Required, long text;
Help text: Use no more than two sentences. Do not include repository locations, security concerns, personal information, implementation details, or incident information)

Assess the application to improve documentation and understand modernization considerations

column1: Create and Publish AIM Master Application Inventory
column26:
Develop a comprehensive master list of all applications owned, managed, or supported within AIM.

The initial inventory will be created using the existing Bifrost extract provided by Dwayne. Once the preliminary list is compiled, it must be validated by AIM managers to ensure all applications are captured and the inventory is complete.

The finalized inventory will be published on the ARO SharePoint site and maintained as a living document that is accessible and editable by all AIM staff.

*Objectives:*

* Establish a single authoritative inventory of AIM applications.
* Validate application data with AIM management teams.
* Identify and add any missing applications not captured in the BiFrost extract.
* Provide a centrally accessible location for ongoing maintenance and updates.
* Ensure changes can be traced to the individual who last updated each application record.

*Scope / Tasks:*

# Obtain the latest BiFrost application extract from Dwayne.
# Review and clean the extracted data as required.
# Create an initial AIM application inventory.
# Define required fields for each application record, including:
#* Application Name
#* Business Owner
#* Technical Owner
#* Support Team
#* Status
#* Last Updated Date
#* Last Updated By
# Engage AIM managers to validate the inventory and identify gaps.
# Update the inventory based on feedback received.
# Publish the inventory to the ARO SharePoint site.
# Configure permissions to allow all AIM staff to view and modify the inventory.
# Ensure the solution captures or displays who last modified each application entry.
# Communicate availability of the inventory and expectations for ongoing maintenance.

*Acceptance Criteria:*

* A master inventory of AIM applications has been created using the BiFrost extract.
* All AIM managers have been consulted to validate the inventory.
* Missing applications identified during validation have been added.
* The inventory is published on the ARO SharePoint site.
* All AIM staff have edit access to maintain the inventory.
* Each application record contains *Last Updated Date* and *Last Updated By* information, either through explicit columns or SharePoint version history.
* Changes to application records can be traced to the individual who made the update.
* The inventory is recognized as the authoritative source for AIM application information.

*Deliverable:*
A centrally managed, collaboratively maintained AIM Application Inventory hosted on the ARO SharePoint site with auditability of record updates and ownership of changes.
